docs.title: Agent Gateway
docs.text:
Version note

Written against agentgateway v1.7.0 (November 2026). The config format has changed between releases. If a field below is rejected, compare it with the standalone docs for your version.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
As soon as you have more than one agent, you also have many MCP servers, several LLM providers and agents calling other agents. Each of these connections needs authentication, rate limits, logging and tracing. Building that into every server doesn't scale.

agentgateway is an open-source proxy (a Linux Foundation project, written in Rust) built for this traffic. Think of it as an API gateway that understands agent protocols:

  • MCP gateway. Federates many MCP servers (stdio, SSE, Streamable HTTP, even OpenAPI services) behind one endpoint.
  • A2A gateway. Proxies agent-to-agent traffic.
  • LLM gateway. Routes to OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock and others, with failover, load balancing and spend controls.
  • Security. JWT, API keys and OAuth for authentication. CEL-based authorization (RBAC) down to individual tools. Rate limiting and TLS.
  • Guardrails. Regex filters, moderation APIs, Bedrock Guardrails, Model Armor and custom webhooks.
  • Observability. OpenTelemetry metrics, logs and traces for every tool call.
flowchart LR
  subgraph Clients
    A1[IDE / Claude / Cursor]
    A2[kagent agents]
    A3[Custom agents]
  end
  A1 & A2 & A3 --> GW[agentgateway<br/>authn · authz · rate limit · OTel]
  GW --> M1[MCP: Kubernetes]
  GW --> M2[MCP: GitHub]
  GW --> M3[MCP: stdio tool]
  GW --> L[LLM providers]
  GW --> AA[Other agents via A2A]

docs.title: Why not a normal API gateway?
docs.text:
MCP and A2A are stateful, session-based JSON-RPC protocols. They often stream, and stdio servers aren't network services at all. A plain HTTP proxy can forward the bytes, but it can't:

  • merge the tool lists of five servers into one,
  • allow list_pods but deny delete_pod for a given user,
  • start a local npx MCP server and expose it over HTTP,
  • trace a single tool call end to end.

agentgateway can do all of these.

docs.title: Install (standalone)
docs.text:
curl -sL https://agentgateway.dev/install | bash -s -- --version v1.7.0
agentgateway --version

Running agentgateway with no arguments creates a starter config at ~/.config/agentgateway/config.yaml. In this guide we pass our own file with -f.

Kubernetes

agentgateway also has a Kubernetes mode with a built-in control plane that is configured through the Gateway API (Gateway, HTTPRoute and so on). Start standalone to learn the concepts, then move to the Kubernetes docs for cluster deployments.

docs.title: Example 1: expose a stdio MCP server over HTTP
docs.text:
Many MCP servers only speak stdio, so they can run only on your laptop. agentgateway can run one and publish it on a port:

config.yaml
mcp:
port: 3000
policies:
cors:
allowOrigins: ["*"]      # lab only; restrict in real deployments
targets:
- name: everything
stdio:
cmd: npx
args: ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"]

agentgateway -f config.yaml

The startup log prints the MCP endpoint and the admin UI address (http://localhost:15000/ui/ in the default setup). Test it with the MCP Inspector:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector
# Transport: Streamable HTTP, URL: http://localhost:3000/mcp

docs.title: Example 2: federate several MCP servers
docs.text:
Add more targets. The gateway merges their tools into one MCP endpoint and prefixes each tool with its target name, so tools with the same name don't clash:

config.yaml
mcp:
port: 3000
targets:
- name: everything
stdio:
cmd: npx
args: ["@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"]
- name: k8s
mcp:
host: http://k8s-mcp.tools.svc.cluster.local:8080/mcp   # remote Streamable HTTP server

Clients (an IDE, a kagent RemoteMCPServer, your own agent) now need only one URL, http://<gateway>:3000/mcp.

docs.title: Securing it
docs.text:
A production gateway should at least:

  1. Authenticate callers with JWTs from your IdP (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta). See Keycloak + Kong for a Keycloak realm setup you can reuse.
  2. Authorize per tool with CEL rules, for example "only members of the sre group may call k8s_* tools; nobody may call delete tools".
  3. Rate limit per client so that a looping agent can't overload a backend.
  4. Restrict CORS to known origins instead of *.
  5. Terminate TLS at the gateway.

The exact policy syntax for JWT and authorization is on the docs' security pages. Check it against your version, because the schema is still changing.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: agentgateway emits OpenTelemetry traces and metrics. Point it at your collector and every agent session becomes a trace: which client called which tool on which backend, how long each step took, and what failed. This fits with the Prometheus & Grafana stack from the Monitoring section.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check Config rejected at startup The schema changed between versions. Compare with the example config shipped in that release. stdio target fails cmd must be on the gateway's PATH (for example, npx needs Node.js). Run the command by hand first. Client connects but sees no tools Wrong transport or path. Use Streamable HTTP and /mcp. Browser client blocked CORS. Add the client's origin to allowOrigins. Admin UI not reachable Check the address in the startup log. The admin port depends on your config.

docs.title: Agentic AI
docs.text: Agentic AI refers to artificial intelligence systems that possess agency, meaning they can make decisions and take actions autonomously to achieve specific goals. Unlike traditional AI systems that operate based on predefined rules or patterns, agentic AI can adapt to changing environments, learn from experiences, and interact with other agents or humans in a more dynamic manner.

docs.title: Chatbot vs. agent
docs.text:
A chatbot answers a question and stops. An agent is given a goal, and it keeps working until the goal is met or it gives up:

Chatbot / copilot Agent Input A prompt A goal ("find out why checkout is returning 500s") Output Text Actions plus a result Steps One model call Many model calls in a loop Touches systems? No, a human copies the answer Yes, through tools (kubectl, APIs, Git, tickets) Who checks the work? The human, every time Guardrails, policies and approval gates

docs.title: The agent loop
docs.text:
Almost every agent framework, from a 50-line script to kagent, runs the same loop:

flowchart LR
  G[Goal] --> P[Plan: LLM decides next step]
  P --> A[Act: call a tool]
  A --> O[Observe: read the tool result]
  O --> M[(Memory / context)]
  M --> P
  P -->|goal met| R[Answer / report]
  1. Plan. The model reads the goal, the conversation so far and the list of tools it may use, then picks the next step.
  2. Act. It calls a tool, for example kubectl get pods -n shop, a Prometheus query or a GitHub API call.
  3. Observe. The tool output is fed back into the model's context.
  4. Repeat until the model decides it has enough to answer, or a limit (turns, time, cost) stops it.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
• Model (the brain). An LLM that can follow instructions and emit structured tool calls. Larger models plan better. Smaller or local models (for example, via Ollama) are cheaper and keep data in-house.
  • Tools (the hands). Functions the agent can call. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is now the common way to expose them, so one Kubernetes or Grafana MCP server works with any agent.
  • Memory. Short-term memory is the context window. Long-term memory is a store the agent can search: runbooks, past incidents, architecture notes.
  • Instructions. The system prompt defines the role ("You are an SRE for the payments cluster"), the boundaries and the expected output format.
  • Guardrails. Limits on what the agent may do: read-only credentials, allow-lists of tools, max turns, spend caps and human approval for anything destructive.

docs.title: Patterns you will see
docs.text:
• Single agent with tools. One model, a handful of tools. Good for focused jobs such as "summarise this alert".
  • Router / orchestrator. A top-level agent hands sub-tasks to specialists (a Kubernetes agent, a Prometheus agent, a Helm agent).
  • Agent-to-agent (A2A). Agents running as separate services call each other over a standard protocol. They can be in different teams or written in different frameworks.
  • Human in the loop. The agent proposes and a person approves before anything changes. This is the right default for production.

docs.title: Where agents help in DevOps
docs.text: Use case What the agent does Incident triage Reads alerts, pulls logs, metrics and traces, and posts a first-pass root cause in the incident channel Kubernetes troubleshooting Explains CrashLoopBackOff, pending pods, failing probes and bad rollouts Change review Reviews Helm/Kustomize diffs and Terraform plans for risky changes Cost and capacity Spots over-provisioned workloads and suggests requests and limits Security Runs scanners, ranks findings and opens tickets (see CAI) ChatOps Answers "what changed in prod in the last hour?" from Slack

docs.title: Risks and how to contain them
docs.text:
An agent has the permissions of its credentials

If the agent's ServiceAccount can delete namespaces, then a confused model, a bad prompt or a prompt injection hidden in a log line can delete namespaces too.

  • Least privilege. Start read-only. Give each agent its own ServiceAccount and scope RBAC to the namespaces it needs.
  • Prompt injection. Treat everything a tool returns (logs, web pages, issue comments) as untrusted data, never as instructions.
  • Hallucinated actions. Require dry runs (kubectl --dry-run=server, terraform plan) and human approval before writes.
  • Cost runaway. Cap turns, tokens and spend per task.
  • Auditability. Log every tool call with inputs and outputs. Put agent traffic through a gateway such as agentgateway so you get a single place for auth, policy and tracing.
  • Data leakage. Know where your prompts go. Use a self-hosted model for sensitive clusters.

docs.title: CAI Cybersecurity Agent
docs.text:
Authorized use only

CAI runs real offensive tooling (scanners, exploit attempts, shell commands). Only point it at systems you own or have written permission to test, inside an isolated lab. Unauthorized testing is illegal in most countries. The project's own docs say it must not be used for cybercrime.

Project status (November 2026)

The open-source CAI repository was archived on 28 August 2026 and is read-only. It gets no new releases, bug fixes or security patches, and the docs describe it as unmaintained attack tooling. Alias Robotics now points users to a commercial successor. The last public PyPI release is 0.5.10. Use CAI to learn and experiment in labs, not as a supported production tool.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
CAI (Cybersecurity AI) is an agent framework from Alias Robotics for building AI agents that do security work: reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation in CTFs, bug bounty triage and defensive analysis. It is built on the OpenAI Agents SDK pattern and talks to 300+ models through LiteLLM, including OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek and local models via Ollama.

It is a useful case study in agentic AI. It has the same loop (plan, act, observe), but the tools are nmap, curl, shell commands and exploit code instead of kubectl.

docs.title: License
docs.text: CAI is not plain MIT. Its LICENSE file mixes MIT-licensed code (derived from openai-agents-python) with proprietary parts under a research-use-only license. Commercial use is prohibited without a commercial license. Read the LICENSE before using it at work.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  U[Operator] --> CLI[cai CLI]
  CLI --> O[Orchestrator / selected agent]
  O -->|handoff| R[Red-team agent]
  O -->|handoff| B[Other specialist agents]
  R --> T[Tools: shell, nmap, curl, code exec...]
  T --> L[(Lab target)]
  O --> LLM[LLM via LiteLLM]
  O --> G[Guardrails · price limit · turn limit]
  • Agents. Specialists with their own prompts and tools. The default is an orchestration_agent that hands work to the others, such as redteam_agent. Run /agent inside CAI to list what your version ships.
  • Tools. Command execution, network tools, code execution and web requests. These are what make CAI powerful and dangerous.
  • Handoffs. Agents can pass a task to a better-suited agent.
  • Human in the loop. The operator can interrupt, redirect or stop the agent at any time.
  • Limits and guardrails. Spend caps, turn and interaction caps, and optional prompt-injection guardrails.
  • Tracing. OpenTelemetry tracing of each step.

docs.title: Set up a lab
docs.text:
Never test against the internet. Build a target you own on an isolated Docker network:

docker network create --internal cai-lab
docker run -d --name dvwa --network cai-lab vulnerables/web-dvwa

Run CAI on the same network, or on a host that can reach only that network. With --internal, the lab has no route to the internet, so the agent can't wander off target. Your CAI host still needs internet access to reach the LLM API, unless you use a local model.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
CAI recommends Python 3.12:

python3.12 -m venv cai_env
source cai_env/bin/activate
pip install cai-framework==0.5.10

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
Create a .env in your working directory. Use placeholders and never commit real keys:

.env
# Model provider (pick one)
OPENAI_API_KEY="<your-openai-key>"
# ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="<your-anthropic-key>"
# OLLAMA_API_BASE="http://localhost:11434/v1"   # local models, data stays on your machine

CAI_MODEL="gpt-4o"                  # or e.g. ollama/qwen2.5:72b
CAI_AGENT_TYPE="redteam_agent"      # default is orchestration_agent

# Safety and cost limits
CAI_PRICE_LIMIT="2"                 # dollars per conversation
CAI_MAX_TURNS="30"
CAI_GUARDRAILS="true"               # prompt-injection guardrails (off by default)

# Observability
CAI_TRACING="true"
CAI_TELEMETRY="false"               # opt out of telemetry

Useful variables:

Variable Default Purpose CAI_MODEL alias1 Model used by the agents CAI_AGENT_TYPE orchestration_agent Which agent starts the session CAI_PRICE_LIMIT 1 Spend cap in dollars. When it is reached, only CLI commands work. CAI_MAX_TURNS / CAI_MAX_INTERACTIONS inf Caps on agent turns and tool actions CAI_GUARDRAILS false Enable prompt-injection guardrails CAI_TRACING true OpenTelemetry tracing CAI_TELEMETRY true Usage telemetry CAI_DEBUG 1 Verbosity (0–2) CTF_NAME, CTF_IP, CTF_SUBNET – Describe a CTF / lab target

Note

The default model alias1 needs a paid Alias key. Set CAI_MODEL to a provider you have a key for, or to an Ollama model.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
CAI_LICENSE_OFF=1 cai     # the open-source build skips the license check this way

The first start can take up to 30 seconds. Inside the REPL:

Command What it does /help, /help topics Built-in help /help var CAI_MODEL Explain a variable /agent List or switch agents /env list, /env set Show or change settings live

Give it a scoped task that names the lab target:

Target: the DVWA container "dvwa" on the cai-lab Docker network (authorized lab).
Scope: only this host. Do not scan other addresses.
Task: enumerate open services and identify the web application and its version.
Report findings with evidence. Do not attempt exploitation.

Watch every command it proposes. Interrupt if it drifts out of scope.

docs.title: Using it responsibly in a DevOps team
docs.text:
• Lab or staging only, on isolated networks, with written scope.
  • Prefer local models (Ollama) when target data is sensitive. Otherwise scan results go to a third-party API.
  • Keep the price and turn limits on. Agent loops are cheap per step but add up quickly.
  • Turn guardrails on. A target can return text crafted to hijack the agent (prompt injection), and the archived project won't fix the known weaknesses.
  • Log everything. Keep the traces as evidence of what was done and when.
  • For continuous, supported checks inside Kubernetes, use maintained scanners such as Kubescape and M9Sweeper. Use CAI-style agents to explore, not as your control.

docs.title: Introduction to MCP
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools and data. Without it, every model needs a custom integration for every system it touches. With it, you write one MCP server for a system (say, your Kubernetes cluster or Grafana) and any MCP-capable AI app can use it.

It is often described as "USB-C for AI": one standard port instead of a drawer full of adapters.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
MCP uses a client–server model built on JSON-RPC 2.0:

Role What it is Example Host The AI application the user interacts with Claude Desktop, an IDE, a custom agent Client A connector inside the host, one per server Created by the host for each server it connects to Server A program that exposes capabilities from one system A Kubernetes, GitHub or Prometheus MCP server 
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> H[Host: AI app + LLM]
  H --> C1[MCP client] --> S1[Kubernetes MCP server] --> K[(Cluster)]
  H --> C2[MCP client] --> S2[Prometheus MCP server] --> P[(Metrics)]

docs.title: What a server can expose
docs.text:
• Tools: actions the model can call, such as get_pods, restart_deployment or query_metrics.
  • Resources: read-only context such as files, logs, config or database rows.
  • Prompts: reusable, parameterized prompt templates.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
• stdio: the host launches the server as a local subprocess. This is simple and good for local tools.
  • Streamable HTTP: the server runs remotely and is reached over HTTP. Use it for shared or hosted servers.

docs.title: Why it matters for DevOps
docs.text:
• One integration, many agents: expose your platform once and reuse it from any assistant or agent framework.
  • Least privilege: each server decides exactly which operations exist, and you can make servers read-only.
  • Auditability: tool calls are structured requests you can log, review and gate behind approvals.

Treat MCP servers like any other privileged service

A server that can kubectl apply is as powerful as the credentials it runs with. Scope its RBAC tightly, prefer read-only tools for exploration, and require human approval for destructive actions.

docs.title: KAgent
docs.text:
Version note

Written against the kagent 1.0.x docs (November 2026). kagent 1.0 changed its resources a lot compared to 0.10.x: it uses the api.kagent.dev/v1alpha3 API group and has no in-place upgrade from 0.10.x. If you run an older version, check kubectl api-resources | grep kagent and kubectl explain agent.spec before copying the YAML below.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
kagent is an open-source framework for running AI agents inside Kubernetes. You define an agent the same way you define a Deployment. You write YAML, kubectl apply it, and a controller turns it into a running agent that can call tools in your cluster.

It is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project, built for DevOps and platform teams who want agents that:

  • are versioned in Git and deployed with GitOps like everything else,
  • use Kubernetes RBAC and namespaces for isolation,
  • reach tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP),
  • can be called from a UI, the CLI or other agents.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  U[User: UI / CLI / A2A] --> C[kagent controller]
  C -->|reconciles| A[Agent]
  A --> T[AgentTemplate<br/>prompt + model + tools]
  A --> H[Harness<br/>runtime]
  T --> MC[ModelConfig<br/>LLM provider]
  T --> R[RemoteMCPServer]
  R --> KT[kagent-tools<br/>k8s, helm, prometheus...]
  KT --> K8S[(Kubernetes API)]
Piece Role Controller Watches kagent resources and runs the agents UI Web console to chat with agents and inspect their tool calls CLI (kagent) Installs kagent, creates sessions and invokes agents AgentTemplate The agent's "brain": system prompt, model config and tool bindings Agent A runnable agent that points to a template and a harness Harness The runtime the agent executes in RemoteMCPServer An MCP endpoint (in or out of the cluster) whose tools agents can use kagent-tools Built-in MCP server with Kubernetes, Helm, Istio, Argo, Prometheus and other tools

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster. The kagent 1.0 docs require Kubernetes 1.37+. For a lab:

    kind create cluster --name kagent --image kindest/node:v1.37.0

  • kubectl and helm

  • An API key for your LLM provider (this guide uses OpenAI)

docs.title: 1. Install the CLI
docs.text:
# Pin the version you tested with
curl -sL https://kagent.dev/install | bash -s -- --version v1.0.0
kagent version

docs.title: 2. Install kagent into the cluster
docs.text:
The CLI is the easiest path. It wraps the Helm charts and reads the provider key from your environment:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="<your-openai-api-key>"
kagent install --namespace kagent

Pass --config kagent-config.yaml to override Helm values.

Installing with Helm instead

The charts are published as OCI artifacts:

helm install kagent-crds oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent-crds \
--version 1.0.0 -n kagent --create-namespace

kubectl create secret generic kagent-openai -n kagent \
--from-literal=OPENAI_API_KEY="${OPENAI_API_KEY}"
helm install kagent oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent \
--version 1.0.0 -n kagent

The chart reads the kagent-openai Secret by default, so no extra value is needed for it. In 1.0 the Helm path also needs a PostgreSQL database and a few supporting charts. Follow the installation guide step by step if you use Helm or GitOps.

docs.title: 3. Check that it is running
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n kagent
kubectl get remotemcpservers -n kagent

You should see the controller, the UI and the kagent-tools pods, plus a RemoteMCPServer named kagent-tool-server.

docs.title: 4. Open the UI
docs.text:
kubectl port-forward -n kagent svc/kagent-ui 8082:8080

Then open http://localhost:8082.

docs.title: Build a read-only troubleshooting agent
docs.text: Our goal is an agent that can look at workloads and explain why they are unhealthy, but cannot change anything.

docs.title: 1. The template: prompt, model and tools
docs.text:
k8s-triage-template.yaml
apiVersion: api.kagent.dev/v1alpha3
kind: AgentTemplate
metadata:
name: k8s-triage
namespace: kagent
spec:
description: Read-only Kubernetes troubleshooting assistant
modelConfig:
name: default-model-config   # created by the installer
systemPrompt: |
You are an SRE assistant for a Kubernetes platform team.
- Investigate using the tools you have. Never guess resource names.
- You are READ-ONLY. If a fix needs a change, write the exact
kubectl or YAML change for a human to apply.
- Finish with: Summary, Evidence, Likely cause, Suggested fix.
tools:
- mcp:
server:
kind: RemoteMCPServer
name: kagent-tool-server
tools:                      # allow-list; leave empty to expose all tools
- k8s_get_resources
- k8s_describe_resource
- k8s_get_pod_logs
- k8s_get_events

Allow-list the tools

The tools list under mcp is the main guardrail. Leave out any create, patch, delete or apply tools and the model cannot call them, however it is prompted. Look up the exact tool names in the UI or with kubectl describe remotemcpserver kagent-tool-server -n kagent for your version.

docs.title: 2. The agent
docs.text:
k8s-triage-agent.yaml
apiVersion: api.kagent.dev/v1alpha3
kind: Agent
metadata:
name: k8s-triage
namespace: kagent
spec:
template:
ref:
name: k8s-triage
harnessRef:
name: default-harness   # see note below

Note

harnessRef must point to a Harness that exists in your cluster. List them with kubectl get harness -n kagent. If none exists, create one as shown in the Your first agent guide.

kubectl apply -f k8s-triage-template.yaml -f k8s-triage-agent.yaml
kubectl get agents -n kagent

docs.title: 3. Try it
docs.text:
Break something on purpose:

kubectl create deployment broken --image=nginx:does-not-exist

Then ask the agent from the CLI:

SESSION_ID=$(kagent agent session create --agent k8s-triage)
kagent agent invoke --session "$SESSION_ID" \

docs.title: KAFKA
docs.text:
Introduction

Apache Kafka is an open-source distributed event streaming platform used by thousands of companies for high-performance data pipelines, streaming analytics, data integration, and mission-critical applications.

Why Kafka? Benefits and Use Cases

  • Data Integration
  • Metrics and Monitoring
  • Log Aggregation
  • Stream Processing
  • Publish-Subscribe Messaging
  • Kafka Architecture – Fundamental Concepts
  • Kafka Topics
  • Kafka Partitioning

How Kafka Partitioning Works

  • Kafka Brokers Kafka brokers are like computer workers in the Kafka system. They store and handle events, manage data partitions, and work together for reliability. Think of them as the backbone of Kafka. So, brokers are the worker bees of the Kafka system, managing events and making sure everything runs smoothly.

Replications

- To ensure data safety, Kafka creates copies of data partitions called leader and follower replicas. When you write data, it goes to the leader, and then both leader and followers automatically replicate the data. If a node fails, another takes over. As a developer, you don't need to worry much about this process. Just know your data is secure and resilient.
Client Applications 
- In Kafka, there are two main types of client applications: producers and consumers. Producers put messages into topics, while consumers read messages from topics. These are the building blocks for working with Kafka. Everything that's not a Kafka broker is essentially a producer or consumer, or both. They're how you connect and work with a Kafka cluster       
Kafka Producers
- The API surface of the producer library is fairly lightweight: In Java, there is a class called KafkaProducer that you use to connect to the cluster. 
Kafka Consumers
- Using the consumer API is similar in principle to the producer. You use a class called KafkaConsumer to connect to the cluster (passing a configuration map to specify the address of the cluster, security, and other parameters).

Kafka Installation

Prerequisite: Java 11 or 17 should be installed on the system
https://kafka.apache.org/documentation.html#java

Download Apache Kafka

https://kafka.apache.org/downloads

  • Extract or untar the downloaded kafka file 

    tar xzvf kafka_2.12-3.5.1.tgz

  • Now test Kafka and move the the kafka directory and use the below command 

bin/kafka-topic.sh

  • Setting the Path 
Open '.bashrc' file using the command: 
vi .bashrc

  • Move to the end and set the path using the command
export PATH=/home/rajivgs/Downloads/webi/kafka_2.12-3.5.1/bin:$PATH

  • To test, run the command from and directory.
kafka-topic.sh

If the below output is shown, it means the path is successfully set. If not, something is wrong.

  • Starting Zookeeper Server on Linux
To start zookeeper, there are following below steps used

Step 1: Move to the and create a new directory 'data'

Step 2: Again, move to the data directory, and make two new directories as 'zookeeper' and 'kafka'.

To run the zookeeper server. Open the zookeeper.properties file, which is located under the config folder. 

 vi config/zookeeper.properties

Edit the value of dataDIr by placing the path of the newly created zookeeper folder.

 zookeeper-server-start.sh config/zookeeper.properties 


zookeeper-server-start.sh config/zookeeper.properties

Move to the 'config' folder, and open server.properties file. 

vi config/server.properties


Edit the value of logs.dir=/path/data/kafka as shown below

Now, run the Kafka server by using the following command: 

  kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties

Creating Kafka Topics Initially, make sure that both zookeeper, as well as the Kafka server, should be started.

kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic topic-name  ||
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic logger --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

Here's a breakdown of the command in short points:

  • kafka-topics.sh: This is the Kafka command-line tool used to manage Kafka topics.

  • --bootstrap-server localhost:9092: Specifies the Kafka broker(s) to connect to. In this case, it's connecting to a Kafka broker running locally on port 9092.

  • --create: Indicates that you want to create a new Kafka topic.

  • --topic logger: Specifies the name of the topic to be created, in this case, the topic name is "logger".

  • --partitions 1: Specifies the number of partitions for the topic. Partitions are the units of parallelism in Kafka. Here, you're creating the topic with 1 partition.

  • --replication-factor 1: Sets the replication factor for the topic. Replication ensures data durability and availability. Here, you're using a replication factor of 1, meaning there's only one copy of each partition's data.

So, the command is creating a Kafka topic named "logger" with a single partition and a replication factor of 1, connecting to a Kafka broker running on localhost at port 9092.

docs.title: Loki
docs.text:
Version note

Written in November 2026. Two recent changes matter:

  • The Loki Helm chart moved to the Grafana Community repo (grafana-community/loki) in March 2026.
  • Promtail reached end of life on 2 March 2026. Use Grafana Alloy to collect logs. Older guides that use Promtail still work, but Promtail gets no updates.

In chart 12.0.0 and later, the SingleBinary deployment mode is called Monolithic.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Grafana Loki is a log aggregation system that works like Prometheus, but for logs. Its key design choice is that it indexes only labels, not the log text. Log lines are compressed into chunks and stored in object storage. Loki is cheap to run and simple to operate, and it fits well with Kubernetes, where every log line already carries labels (namespace, pod, container).

Loki Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Indexes Labels only Full text Storage Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure, filesystem) Local disks / SSD Cost at scale Low High Query language LogQL (PromQL-like) Lucene / KQL / DSL Best at "Show me logs for this pod/app/time" Arbitrary full-text search and analytics

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Node[Each Kubernetes node]
    P1[Pods] --> F[/var/log/pods/]
  end
  A[Grafana Alloy<br/>DaemonSet] -->|discover + label| P1
  A -->|push /loki/api/v1/push| D[Loki<br/>distributor → ingester]
  D --> S[(Object storage<br/>chunks + TSDB index)]
  G[Grafana] -->|LogQL| Q[Loki querier]
  Q --> S
  R[Loki ruler] -->|alerts| AM[Alertmanager]
  • Alloy finds pods, attaches labels and pushes log lines.
  • The distributor and ingester receive the logs, batch them into chunks and flush them to storage.
  • The querier runs LogQL for Grafana.
  • The ruler evaluates alert rules written in LogQL and sends alerts to Alertmanager.

docs.title: Deployment modes
docs.text:
Mode When to use Monolithic (formerly SingleBinary) Labs, dev, small clusters. All components run in one process. Use 3+ replicas for HA. SimpleScalable Being deprecated. Avoid for new installs. Microservices Production at scale. Each component scales on its own.

This guide uses Monolithic with filesystem storage so you can follow it on any cluster. Production setups should use object storage.

docs.title: 1. Install Loki
docs.text:
helm repo add grafana-community https://grafana-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
loki-values.yaml
deploymentMode: Monolithic
loki:
auth_enabled: false            # single tenant; turn on for multi-tenancy
commonConfig:
replication_factor: 1        # required with a single replica
schemaConfig:
configs:
- from: "2024-04-01"
store: tsdb
object_store: filesystem
schema: v13
index:
prefix: loki_index_
period: 24h
storage:
type: filesystem             # use s3 / gcs / azure in production
limits_config:
allow_structured_metadata: true
volume_enabled: true
retention_period: 168h       # 7 days
compactor:
retention_enabled: true
delete_request_store: filesystem
pattern_ingester:
enabled: true
rulerConfig:
enable_api: true
singleBinary:                    # values key kept this name after the mode rename; confirm with `helm show values`
replicas: 1
persistence:
size: 20Gi
# Turn off the components used by the other modes
backend:   { replicas: 0 }
read:      { replicas: 0 }
write:     { replicas: 0 }
ingester:  { replicas: 0 }
querier:   { replicas: 0 }
queryFrontend:  { replicas: 0 }
queryScheduler: { replicas: 0 }
distributor:    { replicas: 0 }
compactor:      { replicas: 0 }
indexGateway:   { replicas: 0 }
bloomPlanner:   { replicas: 0 }
bloomBuilder:   { replicas: 0 }
bloomGateway:   { replicas: 0 }

helm install loki grafana-community/loki \
-n loki --create-namespace -f loki-values.yaml

kubectl get pods -n loki

Pin your versions

Add --version <chart-version> (see helm search repo grafana-community/loki) so that upgrades are deliberate. Run helm show values grafana-community/loki to confirm the keys for the version you install.

Production storage (S3)

schemaConfig:
configs:
- from: "2024-04-01"
store: tsdb
object_store: s3
schema: v13
index: { prefix: loki_index_, period: 24h }
storage:
type: s3
bucketNames:
chunks: my-loki-chunks
ruler: my-loki-ruler
s3:
region: ap-south-1
Use IRSA or workload identity instead of static keys.

docs.title: 2. Ship pod logs with Grafana Alloy
docs.text:
helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
alloy-values.yaml
alloy:
configMap:
content: |
// Find pods on this node only (Alloy runs as a DaemonSet).
// Relies on HOSTNAME being the node name, which the grafana/alloy chart sets
// from spec.nodeName. If no logs arrive, check: kubectl exec ds/alloy -- env | grep HOSTNAME
discovery.kubernetes "pod" {
role = "pod"
selectors {
role  = "pod"
field = "spec.nodeName=" + coalesce(sys.env("HOSTNAME"), constants.hostname)
}
}
// Turn Kubernetes metadata into Loki labels
discovery.relabel "pod_logs" {
targets = discovery.kubernetes.pod.targets
rule {
source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_namespace"]
target_label  = "namespace"
}
rule {
source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_name"]
target_label  = "pod"
}
rule {
source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_name"]
target_label  = "container"
}
rule {
source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app_kubernetes_io_name"]
target_label  = "app"
}
rule {
source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_namespace", "__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_name"]
separator     = "/"
target_label  = "job"
}
}
// Tail logs through the Kubernetes API (no hostPath mounts needed)
loki.source.kubernetes "pod_logs" {
targets    = discovery.relabel.pod_logs.output
forward_to = [loki.process.pod_logs.receiver]
}
loki.process "pod_logs" {
stage.static_labels {
values = { cluster = "dev-cluster" }
}
forward_to = [loki.write.default.receiver]
}
loki.write "default" {
endpoint {
url = "http://loki.loki.svc.cluster.local:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
}
}
controller:
type: daemonset

helm install alloy grafana/alloy -n loki -f alloy-values.yaml
kubectl get pods -n loki -l app.kubernetes.io/name=alloy

Keep label cardinality low

Labels should describe where a log came from (cluster, namespace, app, container), not what it says. Never use request IDs, user IDs or pod IPs as labels. High cardinality is the main way people break Loki. Put those values in the log line or in structured metadata.

docs.title: 3. Add Loki to Grafana
docs.text:
If you followed the Prometheus & Grafana guide, add a data source. Either click through the UI (Connections → Data sources → Loki) or provision it:

datasources:

type: loki

Then open Explore, pick Loki and run {namespace="kube-system"}.

docs.title: 4. LogQL cheat sheet
docs.text:
# All logs for an app
{namespace="shop", app="checkout"}

# Lines containing "error", case-insensitive, excluding health checks
{namespace="shop", app="checkout"} |~ "(?i)error" != "/healthz"

# Parse JSON logs and filter on a field
{app="checkout"} | json | level="error" and status >= 500

# Parse logfmt and show one field only
{app="api"} | logfmt | line_format "{{.method}} {{.path}} {{.duration}}"

# Error rate per app over 5 minutes (a metric from logs)
sum by (app) (rate({namespace="shop"} |= "error" [5m]))

# Top 5 noisiest pods in the last hour
topk(5, sum by (pod) (count_over_time({namespace="shop"}[1h])))

# p95 latency from a logged duration field
quantile_over_time(0.95, {app="api"} | logfmt | unwrap duration_ms [5m]) by (app)

Pattern: stream selector {...} → filters |=, !=, |~ → parsers json, logfmt, pattern → label filters → optional metric wrapper. Filter as early as you can, because it makes queries much faster.

docs.title: 5. Alert on logs
docs.text:
With rulerConfig.enable_api: true, Loki can evaluate Prometheus-style rules written in LogQL. You can also create the same rule as a Grafana-managed alert from Explore.

groups:
- name: checkout-logs
rules:
- alert: CheckoutErrorSpike
expr: sum(rate({namespace="shop", app="checkout"} |= "error" [5m])) > 5
for: 10m
labels:
severity: warning
annotations:
summary: "checkout is logging more than 5 errors/s"

Send these to the same Alertmanager routes as your metric alerts (Google Chat, Slack).

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Retention is enforced by the compactor. The values above keep 7 days (retention_period: 168h with retention_enabled: true). You can override it per tenant or per stream with retention_stream. Also set a lifecycle policy on your object storage bucket as a safety net.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check No logs in Grafana kubectl logs -n loki ds/alloy. Look for push errors. Check the Loki URL and port 3100. entry too far behind / out of order Clock skew, or Alloy replaying old files. Check node time sync. 429 Too Many Requests / rate limited Raise ingestion_rate_mb / ingestion_burst_size_mb in limits_config, or reduce the volume maximum active stream limit exceeded Too many label combinations. Remove high-cardinality labels. Queries time out Narrow the time range, add labels to the selector, put line filters before parsers Ingest fails with 1 replica replication_factor must be 1 Disk filling up Check that compactor retention is enabled. Move to object storage.

docs.title: Conclusion After Setting Up Prometheus and Grafana
docs.text:
Setting up Prometheus and Grafana is a powerful combination for monitoring and visualizing your infrastructure and applications. After completing the setup, you can draw several conclusions and benefits:

  1. Real-time Monitoring: With Prometheus, you have a powerful monitoring system that collects and stores metrics in real-time. This allows you to keep a close eye on the health and performance of your systems.

  2. Alerting: Prometheus provides alerting capabilities, allowing you to set up alerts based on predefined thresholds. You can be notified of issues before they become critical, helping you maintain system reliability.

  3. Historical Data: Prometheus stores historical metric data, enabling you to analyze trends and identify long-term performance patterns. This data can be invaluable for capacity planning and troubleshooting.

  4. Custom Metrics: You can instrument your applications and services to expose custom metrics, giving you deep insights into the specific aspects of your software that matter most to you.

  5. Grafana Dashboards: Grafana offers a user-friendly interface for creating and customizing dashboards that visualize Prometheus data. These dashboards can provide at-a-glance information about the state of your systems.

  6. Data Correlation: Grafana allows you to correlate data from multiple sources and display them in a single dashboard. This helps in diagnosing complex issues that involve multiple components.

  7. Flexibility: Both Prometheus and Grafana are highly customizable. You can adapt them to suit your unique monitoring needs, whether you're running a small web application or a large-scale distributed system.

  8. Community Support: Prometheus and Grafana have vibrant communities with active development and extensive documentation. You can find plugins, extensions, and support readily available online.

  9. Open Source: Both Prometheus and Grafana are open-source projects, meaning you can use them without incurring licensing costs. This makes them an economical choice for monitoring your infrastructure.

  10. Scalability: These tools are designed to scale horizontally, so you can expand your monitoring as your infrastructure grows.

  11. Integration: Prometheus and Grafana can integrate with various other tools and services, allowing you to centralize your monitoring and combine it with other aspects of your DevOps stack.

In conclusion, setting up Prometheus and Grafana provides you with a robust monitoring and visualization solution that empowers you to maintain the health and performance of your systems, make data-driven decisions, and respond proactively to issues. It's a valuable addition to any organization's infrastructure management toolkit. However, to maximize its benefits, ongoing maintenance and tuning may be required to ensure it continues to meet your evolving monitoring needs.

docs.title: During the Karmada Helm chart deployment, a secret containing the karmada-apiserver kubeconfig is created. Extract this kubeconfig file, which is used to configure the karmada-apiserver context.
Extract the Base64 Encoded Kubeconfig:
docs.text:
• There are several ways to achieve this:

  • Using kubectl and yq (recommended if you have yq installed) : 

    kubectl get secret karmada-kubeconfig -n karmada-system -o jsonpath='{.data.kubeconfig}' | base64 -d > karmada.config

Explanation :

  • kubectl get secret karmada-kubeconfig -n karmada-system -o jsonpath='{.data.kubeconfig}' : This extracts the value of the kubeconfig key from the data field of the secret, which is the base64 encoded kubeconfig.
  • base64 -d : This command decodes the base64 string.
  • karmada.config : This redirects the decoded output to a file named karmada.config.

Using kubectl and jq (if you have jq installed) :

kubectl get secret karmada-kubeconfig -n karmada-system -o json | jq -r '.data.kubeconfig' | base64 -d > karmada.config

Explanation :

  • kubectl get secret karmada-kubeconfig -n karmada-system -o json : Retrieves the secret in JSON format.
  • jq -r '.data.kubeconfig' : Parses the JSON and extracts the kubeconfig value (raw, without - quotes).
  • base64 -d : Decodes the base64 string.
  • karmada.config : Redirects the decoded output to the karmada.config file.

Using kubectl, sed, and awk (more manual but works without extra tools) : 

kubectl get secret karmada-kubeconfig -n karmada-system -o yaml | sed -n '/kubeconfig:/,$p' | awk '{if(NR>1)print}' | tr -d ' ' | base64 -d > karmada.config

Explanation :

  • kubectl get secret karmada-kubeconfig -n karmada-system -o yaml : Gets the secret in YAML format.
  • sed -n '/kubeconfig:/,$p' : Extracts lines from kubeconfig: to the end of the file.
  • awk '{if(NR>1)print}' : Skips the first line (which is kubeconfig:)
  • tr -d ' ': Removes leading spaces.
  • base64 -d : Decodes the base64 string.
  • karmada.config : Saves the decoded content to karmada.config.

docs.title: Verify the File (Optional):
docs.text:
• You can verify that the karmada.config file is a valid kubeconfig file by using the kubectl command with the --kubeconfig flag: 
    kubectl --kubeconfig=karmada.config config view

Important Notes:

  • base64 -d : The base64 -d command might be slightly different depending on your operating system. On macOS, you might need to use base64 -D.
  • yq and jq : These are powerful command-line tools for processing YAML and JSON data. If you don't have them, you can usually install them with your system's package manager (e.g., apt-get install yq jq, brew install yq jq).
  • Security: Be mindful of where you store your karmada.config file, as it contains credentials to access your Karmada control plane.

Inside the karamada.config file, you can find the following information: 

apiVersion: v1
clusters:
- cluster: 
    certificate-authority-data: xxx
  server:  https://karmada-apiserver.karmada-system.svc.cluster.local:5443
contexts:
- context:
    cluster: karmada-apiserver
    user: karmada-apiserver
  name: karmada-apiserver
current-context: karmada
kind: Config
preferences: {}
users:
- name: karmada-apiserver
  user: 
    client-certifiticate-date: xxx
    client-key-data: xxx
    name: karmada-apiserver

Here, we the need to use the endpoints in the kubeconfig file to access the Karmada API server. i.e "https://karmada.clustermanager.com" in place of "https://karmada-apiserver.karmada-system.svc.cluster.local:5443"

export KUBECONFIG=karmada.config
kubectl config get-contexts

docs.title: Automated Docker Image Security with Kaniko, Cosign, and Kyverno
Workflow Overview
docs.text:
The workflow for building, signing, and deploying a Docker container in a Kubernetes environment consists of the following key steps:

  1. The process starts with a Dockerfile, used to build a Docker image using Kaniko.
  2. The built Docker image is then signed using Cosign and a private key.
  3. The signed image is verified using Kyverno, a public key, and a cluster policy.
  4. After verification, a pod is created in Kubernetes.

The workflow also integrates with CI/CD tools and container registries; the GitLab container registry is used in the process of the workflow.

Key security components include:

  • Private and public keys for signing and verification
  • Cosign for image signing
  • Kyverno for policy enforcement and signature verification

This workflow represents a secure container deployment process, emphasizing image signing, verification, and policy enforcement before deployment to a Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Build Docker Image
docs.text:
Kaniko, developed by Google, is a popular tool in the software development world. Kaniko is designed to build container images from a Dockerfile, inside a container or Kubernetes cluster, without needing Docker daemon access. This makes creating images in environments like Kubernetes safer, especially when considering the security risks associated with the Docker daemon's privileged mode.

  • It can build accurate Docker images just like Docker would.
  • It does this by executing each command in the Dockerfile in userspace, making a new layer in the filesystem for each command.

So, using Kaniko in your Docker image-building workflow can make it more accurate, secure, and efficient. It's also simple to include in your GitLab CI/CD pipeline.

Understand the difference

Docker: Docker uses a daemon-based approach where the Docker daemon runs on the host machine and builds the image. This requires privileged access, which can be a security concern, especially in Kubernetes clusters. The Docker daemon is a persistent background process that manages Docker images, containers, networks, and storage volumes.

Kaniko: Kaniko is a tool to build container images from a Dockerfile, inside a container or Kubernetes cluster. It doesn't require special privileges, making it more secure for Kubernetes environments.

Now, let's set up the build stage using Kaniko in GitLab CI.

docs.title: Cosign
docs.text: A concise summary of how Cosign can be used to sign and verify Docker images.

docs.title: Cosign: Securing the Software Supply Chain
docs.text:
Key features:

  • Open-source tool to sign, verify, and store containers in OCI registries
  • Part of the Sigstore project to improve software supply chain security
  • Confirms Docker image origin and integrity to ensure safe image use
  • Easily integrates into existing workflows with minimal changes
  • Useful for automating signing in CI/CD pipelines

docs.title: Getting Started with Cosign
docs.text:
1. Create a public/private key pair using the cosign generate-key-pair command.
  2. Store the keys securely in GitLab environment variables or a secrets manager.
  3. Use Cosign to sign Docker images before pushing them to a registry.
  4. Verify signed images before pulling and using them.

docs.title: Keyless Signing with Sigstore
docs.text:
• Cosign supports keyless signing via the Sigstore project.
  • It eliminates the need to manage and rotate private signing keys.
  • Cosign requests a short-lived key pair, records it in a transparency log, then discards it.
  • The key is generated using an OIDC token from the CI/CD pipeline.

Cosign provides a straightforward way to add cryptographic signing and verification to your Docker image workflow, improving the security of your software supply chain.

Now, with the keys created and stored safely, we can set up a GitLab CI job to use Cosign for image signing.

stages:
- sign
sign:
stage: sign
image: docker:latest
needs:
- build-and-push
services:
- docker:dind
variables:
COSIGN_YES: "true"
id_tokens:
SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN:
aud: sigstore
script:
- apk add --no-cache cosign
- echo "Logging in to Docker Hub..."
- echo "$DOCKERHUB_TOKEN" | docker login -u "$DOCKERHUB_USER" --password-stdin "$DOCKERHUB_AUTH_URL"
- echo "Signing the image..."
- IMAGE_REF=$(grep IMAGE_REF build.env | cut -d'=' -f2)
- IMAGE_DIGEST=$(grep IMAGE_DIGEST build.env | cut -d'=' -f2)
- cosign sign "${IMAGE_REF}@${IMAGE_DIGEST}"
- echo "Image signed successfully"
- docker logout "$DOCKERHUB_AUTH_URL"
- echo "Verifying the signed image..."
- cosign verify "${IMAGE_REF}@${IMAGE_DIGEST}" --certificate-identity "$CI_PROJECT_URL//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$CI_SERVER_URL"
- echo "Image verified successfully"
artifacts:
paths:
- build.env

docs.title: Container Signing + Admission Controller
docs.text:
This repository shows an example of how to use GitLab CI to sign container images with Cosign. When new commits are pushed to main, this project will build a new container image and sign it using Cosign.

The Kubernetes admission controller can then be used to prevent unsigned images from running in your Kubernetes cluster. To set up the admission controller for this purpose:

policy.yaml
apiVersion: policy.sigstore.dev/v1beta1
kind: ClusterImagePolicy
metadata:
name: image-policy
spec:
images:
- glob: "**"
authorities:
- keyless:
url: "https://fulcio.sigstore.dev"
identities:
- issuer: https://gitlab.com
subject: https://gitlab.com/bwill/container-signing//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main

docs.title: Image Verification using Cosign
docs.text:
IMAGE_REF="index.docker.io/rajivgs/node-develop"
IMAGE_DIGEST="sha256:b3c2acbad551a2793c0d97073c654a560fb272c8e5310f31c27ea35b4c246f7b"
CI_PROJECT_URL="https://gitlab.com/RajivGS/KCK"
CI_COMMIT_BRANCH="main"
CI_SERVER_URL="https://gitlab.com"
cosign verify "${IMAGE_REF}@${IMAGE_DIGEST}" \
--certificate-identity "$CI_PROJECT_URL//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH" \
--certificate-oidc-issuer "$CI_SERVER_URL"

Signing images with Sigstore

Before signing any image, we need to publish the image to a registry. Cosign does not support signing images that have not been published to a registry. On top of that, you need to have write permission to that registry.

The signature is stored within the same image registry as the main image. The signature carries the identical image digest, with .sig appended to it. Very easy to remember!

Up to this moment, we uploaded the image and the image signature. What's next? Now let's verify it in Kubernetes using Kyverno!

docs.title: Install Kyverno using Helm
docs.text:
Kyverno can be deployed via a Helm chart (the recommended and preferred method for a production install), which is accessible either through the Kyverno repository or on Artifact Hub. Both generally available releases and pre-releases are available with Helm. Full documentation is at kyverno.io.

Note

Kyverno requires kubeVersion >= 1.25.

To install Kyverno with Helm, first add the Kyverno Helm repository, then install the chart:

helm repo add kyverno https://kyverno.github.io/kyverno/
helm install kyverno --namespace kyverno kyverno/kyverno --create-namespace

To secure our Kubernetes clusters, it is essential to ensure that only trusted, signed container images are deployed. Kyverno is a policy engine for Kubernetes that can be used to enforce this security policy.

To use Kyverno to verify container image signatures, we can define a ClusterPolicy CR that specifies the container images to be verified and the required digests. This policy will prevent unauthorized images from being deployed to the cluster.

Here are the steps involved:

  1. Define the specific container image to be verified, either by its tag or SHA.
  2. Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy CR that specifies the container image to be verified and the required digest.
  3. Apply the ClusterPolicy CR to the Kubernetes cluster.

Once the ClusterPolicy CR is applied, Kyverno will intercept all requests to create new pods and deployments. If the container image specified in the request does not have a valid signature or does not match the required digest, Kyverno will deny the request.

docs.title: ClusterPolicy
docs.text:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
name: verify-node-develop-image-signature
spec:
validationFailureAction: Enforce # If image signature verification fails, the Pod is rejected
background: false # The policy is applied during admission control only
rules:
- name: verify-image-signature
match:
resources:
kinds:
- Pod # This rule applies to Pods
verifyImages:
- image: "index.docker.io/rajivgs/node-develop:*"
verifyDigest: true # Verify the image digest (SHA256 hash)
mutateDigest: true # Mutate the Pod spec to include the verified image digest
attestors: # Attestors used to verify the image signature
- entries:
- keyless: # Keyless attestor
# Subject: the GitLab CI/CD pipeline configuration file on the main branch
subject: "https://gitlab.com/RajivGS/KCK//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main"
issuer: "https://gitlab.com"
rekor: # Rekor transparency log used to verify the image signature
url: "https://rekor.sigstore.dev"

Note

When the Kyverno ClusterPolicy verify-node-develop-image-signature is applied to a Kubernetes cluster, it is enforced on any Pod that uses the rajivgs/node-develop Docker image, regardless of whether the image is specified directly in the Pod manifest or in a higher-level resource like a Deployment.

docs.title: Test with an Unsigned Image
docs.text:
Create a manifest that uses the unsigned Docker image:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: node-develop-fail
spec:
containers:
- name: node-develop
image: index.docker.io/rajivgs/node-develop:unsigned

docs.title: Deploy with GitLab CI
docs.text:
Now, to deploy the ClusterPolicy, the signed Docker image, and the unsigned image, we can set up a GitLab CI job:

deploy:
stage: deploy
image:
name: bitnami/kubectl:latest
entrypoint: [""]
needs:
- sign
before_script:
- echo "Kubernetes config file path $KUBECONFIG"
- export KUBECONFIG=$KUBECONFIG
- kubectl config view
script:
- echo "Deploying signed image to Kubernetes cluster..."
- IMAGE_REF=$(grep IMAGE_REF build.env | cut -d'=' -f2)
- IMAGE_DIGEST=$(grep IMAGE_DIGEST build.env | cut -d'=' -f2)
- FULL_IMAGE_REF="${IMAGE_REF}@${IMAGE_DIGEST}"
# Create Kyverno ClusterPolicy manifest
- |
cat << EOF > kyverno-policy.yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
name: verify-node-develop-image-signature
spec:
validationFailureAction: Enforce
background: false
rules:
- name: verify-image-signature
match:
resources:
kinds:
- Pod
verifyImages:
- image: "index.docker.io/rajivgs/node-develop:*"
verifyDigest: true
mutateDigest: true
attestors:
- entries:
- keyless:
subject: "https://gitlab.com/RajivGS/KCK//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main"
issuer: "https://gitlab.com"
rekor:
url: "https://rekor.sigstore.dev"
EOF
# Apply Kyverno ClusterPolicy
- echo "Applying Kyverno ClusterPolicy..."
- kubectl apply -f kyverno-policy.yaml
# Create a temporary deployment YAML
- |
cat << EOF > deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
name: ${DOCKERHUB_IMAGE_NAME}-deployment
spec:
replicas: 1
selector:
matchLabels:
app: ${DOCKERHUB_IMAGE_NAME}
template:
metadata:
labels:
app: ${DOCKERHUB_IMAGE_NAME}
spec:
containers:
- name: ${DOCKERHUB_IMAGE_NAME}
image: ${FULL_IMAGE_REF}
imagePullPolicy: Always
EOF
# Apply the deployment
- kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --validate=false
# Create a manifest file for reference
- |
cat << EOF > manifest.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
name: ${DOCKERHUB_IMAGE_NAME}-deployment
spec:
template:
spec:
containers:
- name: ${DOCKERHUB_IMAGE_NAME}
image: ${FULL_IMAGE_REF}
EOF
# Create unsigned image deployment
- |
cat << EOF > unsigned-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: node-develop-fail
spec:
containers:
- name: node-develop
image: index.docker.io/rajivgs/node-develop:unsigned
EOF
# Attempt to apply unsigned image deployment (expected to fail)
- echo "Attempting to apply unsigned deployment (expected to fail)..."
- kubectl apply -f unsigned-deployment.yaml --validate=false || true
- echo "Deployments created and applied"
- echo "Deployment created and manifest generated"
artifacts:
paths:
- deployment.yaml
- manifest.yaml
- unsigned-deployment.yaml

docs.title: Why use Kaniko instead of Docker?
docs.text:
When getting started, you're likely to run into an error like this:

Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running?

securityContext:
privileged: true
allowPrivilegeEscalation: true

Caching is challenging in Docker, as changes to any layer will invalidate the entire cache for that layer and subsequent layers. Kaniko provides an efficient cache management system where only the necessary layers are invalidated, leading to better cache utilization and faster builds.

docs.title: Comparison between Docker and Kaniko
docs.text: Aspect Docker Kaniko Build process Monolithic, performed inside Docker daemon Distributed, each step executed in separate container Privileged access Requires privileged access to Docker daemon Doesn't require privileged access Build context Entire project directory sent to Docker daemon Users can define specific files/directories Rebuild trigger Changes in project directory trigger complete rebuild Only rebuilds necessary parts that have changed Build performance Can be slower due to intermediate containers and layers Faster due to incremental build process Build environment Tightly coupled to host machine More isolated and reproducible Compatibility May encounter issues when moving between environments Consistent builds across different platforms Cache management Maintains cache of intermediate layers More efficient cache management system Cache invalidation Changes invalidate cache for that layer and subsequent ones Only necessary layers are invalidated Security Potential risks due to privileged daemon access Additional security from isolated build steps Attack surface Larger due to daemon access requirement Reduced, eliminating need for privileged access

docs.title: How does Kaniko enhance security in the build environment?
docs.text: Kaniko eliminates the need for a Docker daemon, reducing potential security risks in the build environment by executing each command in userspace, creating a new filesystem layer for each command.

docs.title: What is the primary function of Cosign in this pipeline?
docs.text: Cosign helps ensure the integrity and provenance of Docker images by signing them, verifying their source, and preventing tampering. It integrates well with existing workflows and can be automated as part of a CI/CD pipeline.

docs.title: How does Kyverno enforce image signing policies?
docs.text: Kyverno is a Kubernetes policy management tool that helps enforce best practices within the cluster. It can verify image signatures, ensuring only properly signed images are used. Kyverno policies can be defined to verify image signatures and enforce the use of signed images.

docs.title: What are the benefits of this automated pipeline?
docs.text: The automated pipeline offers improved security, enhanced efficiency, and increased consistency. It ensures that only signed and verified images are deployed, reducing the risk of deploying tampered or unauthorized images.

docs.title: How can you monitor the health and status of the automated processes?
docs.text: You can monitor the health and status of the automated processes using tools that provide visibility and reporting on the security posture of your Docker images across the organization. This includes monitoring the build, sign, and verify stages to ensure they are running smoothly and efficiently.

docs.title: How does this pipeline integrate with your existing DevOps toolchain and CI/CD workflows?
docs.text: The pipeline integrates seamlessly with GitLab CI/CD pipelines, allowing for the automation of the build, sign, and verify process. This integration ensures that the pipeline is part of your broader DevOps workflow and can be managed and updated centrally.

docs.title: Scalability and Performance
docs.text:

  • Cosign integrates well with existing workflows and can be automated as part of a CI/CD pipeline, allowing it to handle the volume of image signings required.
  • Kyverno is a Kubernetes-native policy management tool that can scale with your infrastructure, enforcing image signing policies consistently across all environments.

  • Use tools like Argo CD to manage and synchronize the Kyverno policies across your environments, ensuring they are up-to-date and compliant with your security standards.
  • Regularly review and update the policies to adapt to changing security requirements and best practices.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: KEDA is a single-purpose and lightweight component that can be added into any Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: How KEDA Works
docs.text:
KEDA performs three key roles within Kubernetes:

  • Agent: KEDA activates and deactivates Kubernetes Deployments to scale to and from zero on no events. This is one of the primary roles of the keda-operator container that runs when you install KEDA.
  • Metrics: KEDA acts as a Kubernetes metrics server that exposes rich event data like queue length or stream lag to the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to drive scale out. It is up to the Deployment to consume the events directly from the source. This preserves rich event integration and enables gestures like completing or abandoning queue messages to work out of the box. The metric serving is the primary role of the keda-operator-metrics-apiserver container that runs when you install KEDA.
  • Admission Webhooks: Automatically validate resource changes to prevent misconfiguration and enforce best practices by using an admission controller. As an example, it will prevent multiple ScaledObjects from targeting the same scale target.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: KEDA works in conjunction with the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, external event sources, and Kubernetes' etcd data store.

docs.title: Event Sources and Scalers
docs.text: KEDA has a wide range of scalers that can both detect if a deployment should be activated or deactivated, and feed custom metrics for a specific event source. See the list of available scalers.

docs.title: Custom Resources (CRD)
docs.text:
When you install KEDA, it creates four custom resources:

  • scaledobjects.keda.sh
  • scaledjobs.keda.sh
  • triggerauthentications.keda.sh
  • clustertriggerauthentications.keda.sh

These custom resources enable you to map an event source (and the authentication to that event source) to a Deployment, StatefulSet, Custom Resource or Job for scaling.

  • ScaledObjects represent the desired mapping between an event source (e.g. RabbitMQ) and the Kubernetes Deployment, StatefulSet or any Custom Resource that defines a /scale subresource.
  • ScaledJobs represent the mapping between an event source and a Kubernetes Job.
  • A ScaledObject/ScaledJob may also reference a TriggerAuthentication or ClusterTriggerAuthentication, which contains the authentication configuration or secrets to monitor the event source.

docs.title: Architecture of Kubescape
docs.text:
The main components of the Kubescape architecture are:

  • Scanner:

    This is the core component of Kubescape. It scans the Kubernetes cluster and identifies potential security risks and vulnerabilities. It uses different techniques to analyze the Kubernetes configuration and resources, such as identifying misconfigured network policies, insecure container images, and non-compliant Kubernetes objects.

  • Policies:

    Kubescape uses a set of predefined policies to evaluate the Kubernetes environment. These policies are customizable and can be modified to suit the specific security requirements of an organization. The policies are written in YAML and can be easily extended to include additional checks.

  • Result:

    The results component of Kubescape provides a detailed report of the security risks and vulnerabilities identified during the scan. It categorizes the findings based on their severity and provides remediation steps for each issue.

  • Web interface:

    Kubescape comes with a web interface that allows users to interact with the tool and view the scan results. The interface provides an easy-to-use dashboard that summarizes the scan findings and allows users to drill down into specific issues.

  • API:

    Kubescape also exposes an API that can be used to integrate with other security tools and automate the scanning process. The API can be used to trigger scans, retrieve scan results, and perform other actions programmatically.

docs.title: Usage of Kubescape
docs.text:
• Security auditing:

    Kubescape can be used to audit the security of a Kubernetes environment by scanning for security risks and vulnerabilities. It can help security teams to identify potential security issues and take the necessary steps to remediate them.

  • Compliance testing:

    Kubescape can also be used to test Kubernetes clusters against compliance standards such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or SOC 2. It can help organizations to ensure that their Kubernetes environments are compliant with industry standards and regulations.

  • DevOps integration:

    Kubescape can be integrated into the DevOps pipeline to perform security checks automatically. This can help organizations to ensure that their Kubernetes deployments are secure and compliant before they are deployed.

  • Continuous Monitoring:

    Kubescape can be used to continuously monitor the security of a Kubernetes environment by running scheduled scans. This can help organizations to detect and remediate security risks and vulnerabilities in a timely manner.

docs.title: Keycloak + Kong: JWT authentication for your APIs
docs.text:
Version note

Tested with Keycloak 26.x and Kong Gateway 3.9 (OSS), DB-less mode, November 2026. Kong's openid-connect plugin is Enterprise-only. This guide uses the bundled open-source jwt plugin, which validates Keycloak's RS256 tokens with the realm's public key.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Keycloak is the identity provider. It authenticates users and services and issues signed JWT access tokens.
  • Kong Gateway is the API gateway. It sits in front of your services and rejects requests that don't carry a valid token.

Your services don't need to know anything about OAuth. Kong checks the token at the edge, so only authenticated requests reach the backend.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant K as Keycloak
  participant G as Kong (jwt plugin)
  participant S as Upstream service
  C->>K: POST /realms/demo/protocol/openid-connect/token<br/>(client_credentials)
  K-->>C: access_token (JWT, RS256, iss=.../realms/demo)
  C->>G: GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
  G->>G: find consumer credential where key == iss<br/>verify RS256 signature + exp
  G->>S: forward request
  S-->>C: 200 OK

docs.title: How Kong's JWT plugin matches a token
docs.text:
This is the part that trips most people up, so it helps to understand it first:

  1. Kong reads the token's iss claim. The claim it reads is set by key_claim_name, which defaults to iss.
  2. It looks for a consumer JWT credential whose key equals that value exactly.
  3. It verifies the signature with that credential's rsa_public_key, using the credential's algorithm (RS256).
  4. It checks the claims listed in claims_to_verify (we use exp).

For Keycloak, iss is the full realm URL, for example http://keycloak:8080/realms/demo. The credential's key must be exactly that string.

docs.title: 1. Run Keycloak and Kong
docs.text:
docker-compose.yaml
services:
keycloak:
image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0
command: start-dev
environment:
KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: admin
KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: change-me      # lab only
KC_HOSTNAME: http://keycloak:8080           # fixes the issuer, see Troubleshooting
ports: ["8080:8080"]
kong:
image: kong:3.9
environment:
KONG_DATABASE: "off"
KONG_DECLARATIVE_CONFIG: /kong/kong.yaml
KONG_PROXY_LISTEN: 0.0.0.0:8000
KONG_ADMIN_LISTEN: 0.0.0.0:8001
volumes:
- ./kong.yaml:/kong/kong.yaml:ro
ports: ["8000:8000", "8001:8001"]
httpbin:
image: kennethreitz/httpbin

Add 127.0.0.1 keycloak to your /etc/hosts so that your machine and the containers use the same hostname for Keycloak. This keeps the iss claim the same everywhere.

docs.title: 2. Configure Keycloak
docs.text:
In the admin console (http://keycloak:8080, log in as admin):

  1. Create a realm called demo.
  2. Create a client called orders-api-client:
    • Client authentication: On (confidential client)
    • Service accounts roles: On (enables client_credentials)
    • Standard flow: Off (machine-to-machine only)
  3. Copy the client secret from the Credentials tab.

  4. Get the realm's public key:

    curl -s http://keycloak:8080/realms/demo | jq -r .public_key

    This prints the bare base64 key. Kong needs it in PEM form, so wrap it like this:

    -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA...
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----

docs.title: 3. Configure Kong with decK (declarative)
docs.text:
kong.yaml
_format_version: "3.0"
services:
- name: orders
url: http://httpbin:80
routes:
- name: orders-route
paths: ["/orders"]
plugins:
- name: jwt
config:
key_claim_name: iss          # default, shown for clarity
claims_to_verify: [exp]
header_names: [authorization]
consumers:
- username: keycloak-demo-realm
jwt_secrets:
- key: http://keycloak:8080/realms/demo   # must equal the token's iss exactly
algorithm: RS256
rsa_public_key: |
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA...
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----

docker compose up -d
# After editing kong.yaml:
docker compose restart kong
Running Kong on Kubernetes?

With the Kong Ingress Controller, the same setup becomes:

  • a KongPlugin (plugin: jwt) attached to your Ingress or HTTPRoute with the konghq.com/plugins annotation,
  • a KongConsumer with credentials: [keycloak-jwt],
  • a Secret labelled konghq.com/credential: jwt that holds key, algorithm: RS256 and rsa_public_key.

docs.title: 4. Test it
docs.text:
# No token → 401
curl -i http://localhost:8000/orders/get

# Get a token from Keycloak
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://keycloak:8080/realms/demo/protocol/openid-connect/token \
-d grant_type=client_credentials \
-d client_id=orders-api-client \
-d client_secret="<client-secret>" | jq -r .access_token)
# Inspect the claims: check that iss matches the consumer key
echo "$TOKEN" | jq -R 'split(".")[1] | @base64d | fromjson | {iss, exp, azp}'   # jq 1.6+
# With token → 200
curl -i http://localhost:8000/orders/get -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Kong adds X-Consumer-Username: keycloak-demo-realm to the upstream request. httpbin echoes it back, so you can see the match.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Authorization, not just authentication. The jwt plugin only proves that the token is valid. To check roles or scopes, add a plugin such as acl (map Keycloak clients to Kong consumer groups) or a policy engine (OPA). You can also check realm_access.roles in the service itself.
  • Key rotation. When Keycloak rotates the realm key, the old public key in Kong stops matching. Automate the update by fetching /realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/certs in CI and running deck gateway sync.
  • Rate limiting per client. Each Keycloak realm or client becomes a Kong consumer, so you can attach rate-limiting per consumer.
  • The same pattern for agents. Agent Gateway can validate the same Keycloak tokens in front of MCP servers.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Kong response Cause Fix 401 No credentials found for given 'iss' The token's iss does not equal the consumer's key. This is the most common failure. Decode the token and copy iss exactly, including scheme, host, port and /realms/<realm>, with no trailing slash. Make clients and Kong reach Keycloak by the same hostname, or set KC_HOSTNAME. 401 Invalid signature Wrong or stale public key, or not in PEM form Fetch public_key again and wrap it in BEGIN/END PUBLIC KEY. Check that the key wasn't rotated. 401 Unauthorized (no detail) No Authorization: Bearer header Check header_names and how the client sends the token 401 token expired exp is in the past Get a new token. Check clock sync. Keycloak's default access-token lifetime is 5 minutes. 401 Invalid algorithm The credential's algorithm doesn't match the token's alg Keycloak signs with RS256 by default. Set algorithm: RS256. Works with curl, fails from the app The app requests tokens through a different Keycloak URL, so iss differs Use one public Keycloak hostname for all clients

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Traefik is based on the concept of EntryPoints, Routers, Middlewares and Services.

The main features include dynamic configuration, automatic service discovery, and support for multiple backends and protocols.

EntryPoints: EntryPoints are the network entry points into Traefik. They define the port which will receive the packets, and whether to listen for TCP or UDP.

Routers: A router is in charge of connecting incoming requests to the services that can handle them.

Middlewares: Attached to the routers, middlewares can modify the requests or responses before they are sent to your service

Services: Services are responsible for configuring how to reach the actual services that will eventually handle the incoming requests.

docs.title: How to rotate and renew expired Contour secrets (contourcert and envoycert)
docs.text: The purpose is to provide a detailed guide on how to rotate and renew expired secrets (contourcert and envoycert) under projectcountour namespace. It includes a step-by-step workaround, prerequisites, and verification steps.

docs.title: Symptoms:
docs.text: • Envoy (pods with name starting with "projectcontour-envoy-") pods under projectcontour namespace show restarts.

docs.title: Example 1
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n proejctcontour

NAMESPACE        NAME                                     READY  STATUS    RESTARTS  AGE  
projectcontour   projectcontour-contour-c476b465b-b5bvn    1/1   Running    1        16h  
projectcontour   projectcontour-contour-c476b465b-jkhsd    1/1   Running    1        16h                    
projectcontour   projectcontour-envoy-wegsv                1/2   Running    161      16h          
projectcontour   projectcontour-envoy-sd7xc                1/2   Running    161      16h      
projectcontour   projectcontour-envoy-u9hac                1/2   Running    162      16h

  • The secrets (contourcert and envoycert) in projectcontour namespace are expired.

docs.title: Example  2
docs.text:
kubectl  get secret -n projectcontour envoycert -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates
notBefore=Jul 24 19:11:31 2023 GMT
notAfter=Jul 26 19:11:31 2024 GMT

kubectl  get secret -n projectcontour contourcert -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates
notBefore=Jul 24 19:11:31 2023 GMT
notAfter=Jul 26 19:11:31 2024 GMT

  • The log for envoy pods in the projectcontour namespace (pods with name starting with "projectcontour-envoy-") reports TLS errors, such as: 

      kubectl  logs -n projectcontour <envoy pod name>

  • [2024-07-26 16:32:01.575][1][warning][config] [bazel-out/k8-opt/bin/source/common/config/_virtual_includes/grpc_stream_lib/common/config/grpc_stream.h:101] StreamListeners gRPC config stream closed: 14, upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection failure, transport failure reason: TLS error: 268435581:SSL routines:OPENSSL_internal:CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED

docs.title: Cause
docs.text: • The secrets (contourcert and envoycert) are used for internal gRPC communication between Contour and Envoy.

docs.title:
Update the contour and under all the resources defined in "contour_certgen_job.yaml" which has following tags: 
"helm.sh/chart: contour-<version>"
"image: docker.io/bitnami/contour:<image_version>"
You can get the current version by running "kubectl describe" on contour deployment/pods.

Run the following commands from manager node to rotate/renew the expired contourcert/envoycert (you can run these commands on the control plane node, there is no need to pass kubeconfig option in that case):

1. Take backup:
    kubectl get secret -n projectcontour contourcert -o yaml > contourcert-backup.yaml
  kubectl get secret -n projectcontour envoycert -o yaml > envoycert-backup.yaml

2. Delete current contourcert and envoycert:
   kubectl delete secret -n projectcontour envoycert contourcert

3. Generate new contourcert and envoycert :
    kubectl apply -f <path>/contour_certgen_job.yaml -n projectcontour

4. Verify that the new contourcert/envoycert was generated:
    kubectl get secret -n projectcontour
